newsitem.title: USA: NYC bar eyes revised "pay-to-play" policy in Jan.
newsitem.headline: NYC bar eyes revised "pay-to-play" policy in Jan.

text.p: The New York City bar association plans to draft a revised policy statement on "pay-to-play" for lawyers in the next month and hopes to present it to the American Bar Association for a vote in August, the group's general counsel said.
"Pay-to-play" is the practice of giving political contributions to state and local government candidates in return for municipal bond business.
The Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board restricts the practice by bond firms, but has no jurisdiction over bond lawyers.
Last year, the prestigious Association of the Bar of the City of New York approved tough curbs on pay-to-play and asked ABA delegates meeting in Orlando last August to adopt the resolution.

But the New York bar withdrew the resolution after ABA members said they needed more time to review the proposal. The New York bar then formed a working group with ABA committee leaders to study the issue.

Alan Rothstein, general counsel for New York's bar, told Reuters in a telephone interview today that his group will circulate "a new, revised resolution" in the next few weeks and present it to ABA at its annual meeting in August 1997.

New York's bar originally wanted ABA delegates to vote on the plan at their 1997 midyear meeting scheduled late this month and in early February in San Antonio. But Rothstein said lawyers need more time.
"We didn't want to rush something in February when it will be in much better shape in August," Rothstein said. "It takes a while to get feedback."

He stressed, however, that his group's basic proposal will remain intact. "The principle is still the same - somebody cannot do municipal finance business within two years after making a contribution to the public official with whom the firm wants to do business."
Rothstein noted that ABA does not have authority to enforce such recommendations in state courts. So, the resolution could recommend to state courts that they require lawyers to follow the plan.

Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt has called on groups representing municipal bond lawyers, issuers and financial advisers to take strong positions barring pay-to-play in the municipal bond market.
